title: The Qur'an as first source
hook: every school begins with the Qur'an

segments.voice: Yesterday, shari'ah, and your line: the path and the map. Did you hear the word used, and did the speaker mean the path or a map? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

"O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." That's a verse of law, in Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an. Listen to what's packed into one breath. Who it speaks to. A command. A link to people who came before. And a reason. When the schools of law sit down to work out a ruling, this is where they start: with the book, read slowly, phrase by phrase. Today: the Qur'an as first source.
screen: `O YE WHO BELIEVE!` → `A COMMAND, A LINK, A REASON.` → `WHERE THE SCHOOLS START.`

segments.voice: First, why first. Muslims hold the Qur'an to be the speech of Allah, and the schools of law, Sunni and Shia, begin their reasoning there. A well-known report puts it as a scene. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is sending Mu'adh ibn Jabal to Yemen as a judge, and asks him how he'll judge. By the Book of Allah, Mu'adh says. And if it isn't there? By the sunnah. And if it isn't there? By my own careful reasoning. Hadith critics have graded that report differently, exactly the kind of thing the last block taught us to notice. But the order it describes is the order the schools teach. Second, where the law sits. The verses of law aren't gathered into one chapter. They sit among stories, prayers, promises and warnings, so a jurist reads the whole book to find them. Third, the reasons. Like the fasting verse, a ruling often comes with its purpose attached: that ye may ward off evil. Jurists pay close attention to those purposes, and later in this block that attention becomes a method of its own. Fourth, the limits of a single source. The Qur'an commands prayer again and again, but it doesn't spell out every movement of it. For that, the scholars turn to the second source, which is tomorrow. And since today ends a week, look back along it. Careful with the weak. Forty to carry. Explained for us. With a teacher. The chain held. The path and the map. Every one of those was about how carefully a tradition handles its sources. Today the first of them: the book first.
screen: `BOOK, THEN SUNNAH, THEN REASONING.` · `LAW AMONG THE STORIES.` · `A RULING WITH ITS REASON.` · `THE BOOK DOESN'T STAND ALONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: read a verse of law, slowly, in pieces. Settle, and breathe. O ye who believe: who it speaks to. Breathe. Fasting is prescribed for you: the command. Breathe. Even as it was prescribed for those before you: a link to others. Breathe. That ye may ward off evil: the reason. Say each piece once more, with a breath between. Then rest on the last piece, the reason, and let one question sit with you: what is this command for? The bell holds the time.
The Qur'an as first source. The schools of law begin their reasoning with the Qur'an, its verses of law read closely, reasons and all. Today's word.
screen: `THE QUR'AN AS FIRST SOURCE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the book first. Today, when a question comes up, ask what the source itself says before asking what anyone thinks about it. Tomorrow: the sunnah as second. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: In Islamic law, scholars of the Sunni and Shia schools begin with the Qur'an when working out a ruling, reading its verses of law closely along with their context and purposes.
